repos.title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
repos.paper_summary: This paper proposes a framework for testing how added context changes the behavior of LLM social agents. It defines five context conditions, from minimal context to normative decision grounding, and a criterion called selective robustness: stability under meaning-preserving prompt changes, plus a prespecified directional response to changes in the social world. In a Prisoner's Dilemma-like hospital supply game run on GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra, each cell was queried ten times, and transfer probability was computed from token log-probabilities. Grounded conditions produced strong world responsiveness. Sol reached 85.9 points under descriptive grounding and 92.0 under normative grounding, with surface sensitivity of 3.7 and 3.9 points. Terra's local normative alternative-prose cell gave 89.9% transfer, versus at most 0.9% for the other surfaces. Limitations include one scenario, two models from one family, no human check of semantic equivalence, and grounded prompts that also add world detail, so salience and grounding are confounded.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Richer agent context may reduce brittleness, but context enrichment is poorly defined, so the paper proposes selective robustness for controlled tests.

digest_headlines.heading: Framework
digest_headlines.headline: Five prompt conditions are built by substitution, and selective robustness is defined by surface invariance plus prespecified world responsiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: In a hospital supply game with two models, grounded conditions produce strong world responsiveness, but Terra stays sensitive to surface form.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Outlook
digest_headlines.headline: Context construction should be treated as experimental design, though the pilot's single scenario and two models limit generalization.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the AI use statement, game and prompt materials, execution details, and additional result tables.

repos.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
repos.paper_summary: NorthCUA is a family of computer-use agent models (Nano 9B, Mini 35B, Pro 397B, all built on Qwen3.5), trained through an integrated pipeline that collects and learns from desktop and web GUI experience. The NorthCUA Harness runs tasks in isolated workspaces, records each step, and checks outcomes with task verifiers and an evaluator. The Experience Flywheel builds executable tasks and curates verified trajectories. Staged Learning applies GUI mid-training, supervised fine-tuning on verified long workflows, and joint desktop-web reinforcement learning with GRPO, using verifier outcomes as rewards. Recursive self-improvement reuses tested skills and saved verified milestones on unsolved tasks. The authors report that Pro outperforms Qwen3.8-Max and Kimi-K3 on two grounding benchmarks, OSWorld-Verified, and WebArena-Verified, and that Mini surpasses Kimi-K3 on OSWorld-Verified. NorthCUA-Ultrafast, built on pre-RL Nano with a head that selects finite actions directly, completes matched successful WebArena-Verified tasks 2.3× faster on average than full generation. Stated limitations include unfamiliar software and changing interfaces, verifier coverage, sparse terminal feedback over long workflows, and indirect prompt injection.

digest_headlines.heading: 1Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: NorthCUA couples executable task construction, agent execution, and policy training so experience from software use feeds back into the policy.

digest_headlines.heading: 2Scope and System Overview
digest_headlines.headline: The paper separates single-step control grounding from end-to-end desktop and web tasks, each with fixed requests and completion checks.

digest_headlines.heading: 3NorthCUA Harness: Full-Lifecycle Infrastructure for Computer Use
digest_headlines.headline: The NorthCUA Harness runs each attempt through a shared runtime, long-horizon context management, outcome evaluation, and batch collection with preserved records.

digest_headlines.heading: 4Experience Flywheel: Scaling Grounding and Agentic Experience
digest_headlines.headline: The Experience Flywheel builds grounding examples and executable tasks through three construction routes, and retains progress from hard tasks via skills and milestones.

digest_headlines.heading: 5Staged Learning from Scalable GUI Experience
digest_headlines.headline: Staged Learning trains in three stages: broad GUI mid-training, verified long-horizon supervised fine-tuning, and joint desktop–web reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: 6Experiments and Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: NorthCUA-Pro scores 93.3% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 91.0% on OSWorld-G, the highest among systems compared in grounding.

digest_headlines.heading: 7Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: NorthCUA differs from prior systems by integrating decision-time input preservation and complete-attempt weighting with its harness and experience pipeline.

digest_headlines.heading: 8Limitations and Responsible Use
digest_headlines.headline: Open limits include unfamiliar software, verifier coverage, and terminal-only feedback on long workflows.

digest_headlines.heading: 9Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: NorthCUA reports the highest open-source results across three domains and releases its three models and harness code.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation and information boundaries, grounding and task construction details, training data scale, model identities, and extended case studies.

repos.title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
repos.paper_summary: Drex is a family of four open decision models that return a probability over each question's options without autoregressive decoding. The largest, Drex Max, is a 27B dense multimodal model that reads answers from a readout head with one logit per option code, up to 255 options. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with consistency losses, reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), and vision tuning. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max scores 67.52 on the public suite versus 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0. On Decision Bench v4 it reaches 94.0% accuracy, not significantly different from GPT-6 Sol and 1.6 points below Claude Opus 5.5. In a controlled ablation, RLAF adds 2.0 Decision Index points, and the consistency terms lower the top-1 flip rate from 6.3% to 4.2%. Limitations: all Drex models trail frontier chat models on closed-book knowledge benchmarks such as HLE and GPQA. Max's expected calibration error is 8.4% on questions with 6 to 20 options, and 13% of decisions with six or more options change their top option under reordering.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Decision models read answers as option probabilities without decoding, for option sets supplied at inference time.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related work
digest_headlines.headline: The Drex models sit between option scoring, pointer networks, and calibration work, and each uses a different backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Problem formulation
digest_headlines.headline: A decision request holds a state and typed questions, and the model returns a distribution over each question's supplied options.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Pointer architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Pointer models encode the context once and score each option with a dot product between query and option-end states, with no decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Drex Max: a dense multimodal decision model
digest_headlines.headline: Drex Max removes the causal mask in full-attention layers of a 27B backbone and reads answers from a readout head over option codes.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training combines supervised fine-tuning with consistency losses and reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback, with vision tuning for Max.

digest_headlines.heading: 7 Experimental setup
digest_headlines.headline: Models are compared on Decision Index 0.4.1, Decision Bench v4 and other suites, using Wilson intervals and exact McNemar tests on paired questions.

digest_headlines.heading: 8 Results
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover accuracy, calibration, option order, images and training stages, compared against decision-specialized and frontier chat models.

digest_headlines.heading: 9 Deployment and inference optimization
digest_headlines.headline: Shared prefill, graph capture and kernel changes cut latency, and answer-changing optimizations are accepted only within an accuracy threshold.

digest_headlines.heading: 10 Discussion and limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Stated limits: gaps to frontier chat models on closed-book knowledge, over-confidence in Max, and untested causes of its gains.

digest_headlines.heading: 11 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Drex Max leads the public Decision Index at 67.52, and its gains over the pointer models are not isolated to one design choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, question types and metrics, pointer masks, Drex Max kernel timings, deployment setups and Decision Index scoring.

repos.title: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements
repos.paper_summary: CUA-Master is a training framework for computer-use agents built as two nested data-and-training loops. The outer loop feeds the model's observed weaknesses back into data collection and adds open-world material. The inner loop has two parts. Open-world seeding mines seed tasks and trajectories from instructional videos on YouTube, TikTok, and Bilibili, using transcript cues and frame-change triggers to locate actions. Autocatalytic propagation abstracts seeds into application-level primitives, composes them into single- or cross-application tasks with verifiers, and collects rollouts with snapshot-rollback retries. The agent uses GUI actions and shell CLI commands in one action space. CUA-Master-27B scores 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench, and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam. The text provided contains no baseline numbers, and it ends before the training results, so the claimed gains over other models and across iterations cannot be checked here. The paper notes that video-derived trajectories may contain annotation noise and may not match real executions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Computer-use agent training is limited by narrow, uncontrolled, and unreliable synthetic data, so the paper proposes a nested recursive framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: CUA-Master pairs an outer world-data-model flywheel with an inner data flywheel that mines tutorial videos and synthesizes verifiable tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: CUA-Master-27B scores 80.2, 36.9, 43.9 and 25.0 on four benchmarks, and mixing screen and shell actions beats screen-only execution.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The framework is reported to achieve competitive results and consistent gains across recursive iterations.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related work, training data distribution, domain results, methodology prompts, action space, taxonomy, and limitations.

repos.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
repos.paper_summary: ODE policy learns the dynamics of a robot action, modeling the policy as a neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) whose vector field is conditioned on the observation. Each action is integrated from the previous one at inference, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. In imitation learning, the field is trained by matching integrated action chunks to demonstrations, and a contractive perturbation of chunk start points pulls states back toward the demonstrations. An optional diversity head supports multi-modal behavior. On LIBERO, it reaches 79.2% success after one epoch, against at most 43.2% for baselines. As the action head of π0.5, it reaches 96.0% against 75.5% for flow matching. It generates a chunk 10.8 times faster than flow matching in simulation. It has the highest success rate on all 14 real-world tasks. As the actor of SuperMimic in RL, it ends training with a return of 0.885 against 0.845. Limitations: encoding the binary gripper command as a field state lowers LIBERO success after one epoch from 79.2% to 74.5%. Early model-free RL experiments showed little gain and sometimes a loss. Several analyses use a single seed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Most robot policies map observations to discrete actions and leave continuity to be learned; ODE policy instead learns the action's dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior ODE robot policies fix the vector field's form, and efficiency methods keep direct-action actors, which ODE policy changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Direct-action policies output each action separately, while a neural ODE defines a field integrated over time.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method integrates a learned action field over each chunk, trains it on integrated paths, and adds a sampled diversity offset.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation compares ODE policy with 14 baselines on simulated and real tasks, with shared backbones, data, and training schedules.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation Results
digest_headlines.headline: In simulation, ODE policy learns faster, needs fewer demonstrations, generates actions faster, and keeps multiple behavior modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-World Results
digest_headlines.headline: On four real robots, ODE policy has the highest success rate on each reported task and transfers dexterous skills across labs.

digest_headlines.heading: Ablation Studies
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations show that chunking is essential and that removing the contractive perturbation drops the one-epoch success rate from 79.8% to 58.4%.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Discussion argues continuity built into the policy improves efficiency across scales and suggests three preliminary extensions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists benchmark and robot details, training settings, timing tables, and extra generalization, multi-modal, and ablation results.

repos.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
repos.paper_summary:
TurnWise is a turn-level GRPO framework for streaming video RL that gives each response-or-wait decision its own advantage and weights decisions equally in the loss. For each trajectory, it scores every prefix with all later turns set to silence, subtracts the reward accrued before each turn, and normalizes the remaining return within the rollout group. Turn-mean aggregation averages token losses within each turn, then across turns, so output length does not set a turn's weight. No critic or extra rollouts are needed.

On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, TurnWise reaches 43.56 PAUC on ProactiveVQA, 21.59 Timing F1 on OVO-Timing, and 49.43 average accuracy on StreamingBench, which are 3.96, 3.87, and 0.69 points above the strongest non-TurnWise results. On Qwen3-VL-4B it reports 42.44, 11.15, and 58.96. Adding turn-mean aggregation to turn-level credit cuts repetition from 15.53 to 5.98 relative to credit-only training.

Limitations: experiments cover two Qwen backbones and three benchmarks, and the reward is the fixed PAUC-based scorer from MMDuet2. The alpha sweep tests only four correction strengths.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Shared trajectory-level advantages misassign credit to redundant replies and useful follow-ups in streaming video reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior streaming video methods use trajectory-level GRPO, which broadcasts one advantage across all decision turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Silence-completed prefix scores give each turn a remaining-return advantage, and turn-mean averaging weights every turn equally.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare TurnWise with fine-tuned and reinforcement-learning baselines on three streaming benchmarks using two Qwen backbones.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Discussions
digest_headlines.headline: TurnWise posts the best aggregate scores on all three benchmarks, reaching 43.56 on ProactiveVQA with the 3B backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Turn-level credit without a critic supports higher-quality, better-timed and more selective streaming responses.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix derives the telescoping decomposition, the group-relative correction, the interpolation and warm-up schedule, and the dual-clipping loss.

repos.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
repos.paper_summary: Axion 1.0 is an open agent foundation model trained in three stages: two supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stages, then reinforcement learning (RL), with no mid-training, DPO, or on-policy distillation. Stage I trains on science problems generated from public seeds and made harder using the base model's own solutions. Stage II trains on tool-use questions built by deterministic filter, select, and compute programs over structured databases that are hidden during solving. RL uses GRPO with partial credit for verified intermediate steps. The authors release data construction code, prompts, and training code. On full Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) with website access restricted, the 35B and 122B models score 52.2% and 59.0%. Against Agents-A1 (47.6%), the 35B model is 4.6 points higher on HLE, 5.8 points higher on SEAL-0, and 7.0 points higher on FrontierScience Olympiad. The 122B model reaches 66.7% on FrontierScience Research, above GPT-5.6 Sol's 63.3%, but scores 41.7% on BioMysteryBench, below GPT-5.6 Sol's 47.1%. Limitations: each score is the best of one run, baselines come from mixed sources and tool settings, and the stage-contribution results in Section 4.3 are cut off in the provided text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Axion 1.0 asks whether a three-stage recipe without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization or on-policy distillation can still yield broad agentic capabilities.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Construction
digest_headlines.headline: Both data pipelines build questions with verified reference answers and keep only correctly solved trajectories for training.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training runs two supervised stages then reinforcement learning, with partial credit for verified intermediate steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Under restricted web access the 122B model scores 59.0% on Humanity's Last Exam and 66.7% on FrontierScience Research.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Infrastructure
digest_headlines.headline: Separate infrastructure trains long 128K-token trajectories with sharding and runs asynchronous reinforcement learning with token-consistent rollouts.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Axion differs from related agent, data and training-consistency work by using a simpler two-stage supervised sequence followed by reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that simpler, data-centric pipelines can produce strong agent models, with code and data released.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists supervised and reinforcement learning hyperparameters and three case studies comparing checkpoints across training stages.

repos.title: History Forcing: Distilling History-Dependent Continuations for Long-Horizon Video World Models
repos.paper_summary: History Forcing is a distillation framework for few-step autoregressive video diffusion models that adds a history-dependent correction to the distillation target. For each student chunk, a frozen autoregressive teacher predicts the same noisy chunk with and without extra history. The difference between the two scores, scaled by a weight $\lambda$, is added to the reference score in distribution matching distillation, or to the teacher velocity target in on-policy self-distillation. For long-video generation, the history comes from earlier student chunks. For out-of-sight world modeling, it comes from a fixed-camera teacher rollout. On 15s VBench generation, the variant with a 10s-fine-tuned teacher scores 85.07 quality, versus 84.44 for the baseline without history supervision. On 60s VBench-Long, a 1.3B student reaches an aggregate score of 79.82, above Rolling Forcing (79.22) and LongLive (79.12) and below the 5B LongLive-2.0 (79.90). On the PlayWorld Out-of-sight subset, Evolution Quality rises from 2.35 to 2.70. On MemoBench Real, Object Consistency rises from 58.43 to 62.18. Limitations: long-video experiments use only 1.3B models, world-model experiments use one 5B backbone, and gains are bounded by how well the teacher models temporal dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: History Forcing adds a history-based correction to distillation so long video rollouts keep subjects and scenes consistent.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work adds history through memory or training changes, but leaves the contribution of history implicit in distillation targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Background defines flow-matching velocity, chunk-wise autoregressive factorization, and distribution matching distillation gradients.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: History Forcing adds a history-contrast residual to the reference score for long videos and to velocity targets for revisits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: History Forcing scores highest among 1.3B students on VBench-Long and improves out-of-sight revisit metrics on both benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: History Forcing reduces drift in long videos and keeps object states across out-of-sight gaps, within limits set by the base models.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training, inference and evaluation settings and additional qualitative examples for both applications.

repos.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
repos.paper_summary: VisSearch-Bench is a benchmark of 204 human-written tasks for evaluating visual context management in long-horizon open-web search by multimodal agents. The tasks span five categories: Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide–Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search, across 7 primary and 25 secondary domains. Annotators build each task from public sources with a reference answer and traceable evidence, and automated checks plus human review remove tasks that can be solved without the visual evidence. Accuracy requires the predicted answer to contain all and only the required content. Process Score is the fraction of labeled critical states recovered, averaged over tasks. Across 16 models and agent setups, the best system reaches 26.47% accuracy, a ReAct agent with Kimi-K3. Direct answering by GPT-5.5 scores 6.37%, and ReAct with GPT-5.5 reaches 25.49%. Several open-source models score 0.00% accuracy on the direct setting. The paper states that the benchmark's 204 tasks are a limited sample and that the construction relies on human annotation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Some search tasks use images only to identify an entity, so the paper tests how agents link visual evidence across steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: VisSearch-Bench is the only listed benchmark that covers set answers, evidence links, and partial credit together.

digest_headlines.heading: VisSearch-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Each of 204 tasks is built from public sources with traceable evidence, a locked answer, and human review.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Search lifts accuracy well above direct answering, but the best system still fully solves only 26.47% of tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Verifying multiple objects and combining findings into consistent answers remain open challenges for multimodal search agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related benchmark details, prompts, hyperparameters, release fields, and seventeen case-study trajectories.

repos.title: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360$^{\circ}$ View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments
repos.paper_summary: PhotoGuider is a method for choosing a viewing direction in a 360° panorama and framing a photo within it, using four interpretable photographic tokens (Subject, Composition, Integrity, Aesthetics) computed from pretrained vision models. Compact LightGBM rankers and gates, with about 63k parameters, select and refine crops. A fine-tuned MLLM explainer, distilled from Qwen2.5-VL-7B, produces explanations conditioned on the token measurements. On FCDB and FLMS, the paper reports an average mIoU of 0.811 for the full mode against 0.792 for Venus and 0.789 for Cropper, with average BDE of 0.044. Fine-tuning reduced the explainer's measured contradiction rate from 6.31% to 1.55%. In a 120-participant blind ranking of 100 Poly Haven panoramas, framings were ranked first 53.2% of the time, against 27.3% and 19.5% for two alternatives. Limitations stated by the authors: refinement uses discrete step fractions, and view selection returns a single argmax without user control.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Panoramic framing needs a direction choice before cropping, which PhotoGuider addresses with four interpretable photographic tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior croppers, critics, and view selectors offer scores that are hard to inspect or check against measurements.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: PhotoGuider ranks shortlisted candidate framings with four photographic tokens, then refines the top frame with gated moves.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: PhotoGuider's full mode scores highest average mIoU, 0.811, on two 2D benchmarks and places first in 53.2% of 360° rankings.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors list discrete refinement steps and a single view argmax as limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists token feature definitions, candidate sources, gate details, consultant and explainer settings, and user study analyses.
